summary:
We wanted to draw attention to significant changes in climate and weather that are influencing migration and conflict-related displacement in South Sudan. Humanitarian groups tend to measure South Sudan’s floods by what percentage of the Sudd wetland, a massive wetland in South Sudan formed by the White Nile, lies under water at the height of the seasonal rains. Our team built the South Sudan Trend Explorer, an interactive map of all 79 counties in South Sudan from 2018 to 2025, to show a fuller picture. The tool pairs NASA Earth observation with UN records of hunger, conflict, and displacement. It tests each county’s trends for significance with Sen’s slope and a seasonal Mann-Kendall test, comparing each month with the same month of 2018 to control for seasonality. 

The dry-season record shows a distinct trend. The wet-season flood has held steady since 2019 (p = 0.71), but the water left standing each March rose tenfold, from roughly 800 to 8,300 square kilometres (p = 0.004). That water inundates the seasonal pasture that herders rely on until the rains return. In the counties where flooding most increased, crisis-level hunger rose in tandem. Aid planners can read the February-to-April water level as a warning of hunger months before the next IPC analysis. Interestingly, we also flagged a result of NASA’s Terra satellite changing its timing - when it began to pass over South Sudan earlier in the day, the trend falsely captured ‘significant’ cooling of the ground.
details:
The South Sudan Trend Explorer is a static web map of South Sudan’s 79 counties, month by month from January 2018 to December 2025. A user picks one of 18 climate and environment measures or 10 human measures, then sets the map to show either raw values or each county’s trend. The trend view compares every month with the same month of 2018, which removes the seasonal swing; it colors each county by its Sen’s slope and outlines those whose seasonal Mann-Kendall trend stays significant. Clicking on a county opens its time series, a short profile of its livelihoods and conflict history, an option to compare the trends in the selected variable to another county of the user's choice, and a CSV download for the displayed data. Point layers mark displacement camps, oil wells, health facilities, UN bases, and water points; migration arrows from IOM Event Tracking show where flood-displaced and conflict-displaced people moved.

We used the tool to discover untold stories about the relationship between ecological change and climate change and conflict. We found two particularly interesting, and decision-relevant, stories for policymakers and humanitarian aid groups.

Beyond the findings about flooding in the Sudd, discussed in the summary, the tool surfaced several patterns with direct consequences for humanitarian planning. Floods and fighting displace people on opposite calendars: every year from 2020 to 2025, between 77 and 100 percent of flood displacement fell between June and November, while between 59 and 89 percent of displacement from communal conflict fell between December and May. Families fleeing floods also travel shorter distances; 94 percent stayed within their own county (a median move of 7 kilometres), compared with 72 percent of those fleeing conflict. The same 33 counties received 73 percent of flood-displaced people and 67 percent of conflict-displaced people, so these host communities take in two waves of arrivals each year. Only a third of flood displacement began in the Sudd. Twic, Terekeka, Gogrial West, and Tonj South, all outside the wetland, recorded more flood displacement than most Sudd counties. Within flood-prone counties, years with more local rain brought less flooding (ρ = −0.43), consistent with water arriving down the White Nile from Lake Victoria. In market towns, sorghum prices rose in years when more land stayed flooded through the dry season (p = 0.0001).

Over the same period, the number of aid organisations working in Sudd counties fell by 32 percent between 2019 and 2025, against 7 percent elsewhere. A check showed MODIS fire counts falling 38 percent outside the Sudd. Our team also used the tool to set aside hypotheses the data could not support, including a theory that there would be a link between oil infrastructure and health outcomes or that there would be a spillover of drought conditions causing cattle raid conflict, leading to displacement from the Sudd to neighbouring counties.

The intended users are students and members of the public learning to read Earth system trends, along with humanitarian planners. For planners, the February-to-April water level in the Sudd tracks the following year’s hunger, months before the next IPC analysis. For students, the tool models two questions to ask of every trend: whether it is significant, and whether the instrument that measured it changed. It allows students to understand an important conflict, and policy dilemma facing countries like the USA tasked with deploying aid, with not only the relevant historical context - displayed in the tool as the user slides through time - but also with the ecological context that clearly displays the human impacts of climate change.

Its creative contribution lies in measuring the seasonal minimum, which reporters and aid agencies rarely track, and in seeing the interrelationships between climate and human variables. Our team weighed several limits. Hunger and water move together most strongly in Rubkona and Guit, where Bentiu’s displacement camp has also drawn in families since 2021, so we describe the hunger finding as an association, not a cause. We struggled with data availability, because IPC analyses are irregular - for example, no county survey round was conducted in 2021. Sentinel-1 radar can sometimes miss water beneath swamp vegetation, an important factor in the Sudd, so we integrated other forms of measurement like the gravimetric GRACE-FO water measureemtns and MODIS reflectance to increase the fidelity of our data.

We used many coding tools, including Python (pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, rasterio), and Google Earth Engine. We accessed data using tools like Microsoft Planetary Computer, NASA AppEEARS, NASA FIRMS, and NASA POWER for data processing. We made the app using programming tools like static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript site built with Leaflet and Chart.js. The final product is open-source and hosted on GitHub.
